name: Lakota (Teton division of the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ)
notes: The Očhéthi Šakówiŋ ("Seven Council Fires") splits into three linguistically distinct divisions — Dakota (Eastern/Santee), Nakota (Yankton/Yanktonai, itself a probable historical mislabel since "Nakota" properly names the distinct Assiniboine/Stoney languages), and Lakota (Teton, western division) — not one flattenable group; this entity covers Lakota (Teton) only. "Sioux" is a French-shortened form of an Ojibwe exonym (Nadouessioux), transmitted via Algonquian speakers, not self-applied, though it persists in many tribal governments’ own official English names today (e.g. Oglala Sioux Tribe) and is not a cleanly rejected term. Documented historical TRANSFORMATION, not a timeless baseline: 17th-century Lakota/Dakota lived as Minnesota woodland/prairie-edge people; the horse-and-bison-mounted Plains economy iconically associated with the Lakota took shape only from c. 1700 onward (Richard White 1978; Pekka Hämäläinen, Lakota America, Yale UP 2019), following westward migration driven substantially by warfare with the Ojibwe over firearms access.
